utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I'll be acting as the Presiding Judge today. Mr. Cayley is in charge, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, my learned friends for the Defence. The next witness, Judge Riad, is a protected witness. So prior to the witness entering the courtroom, with your permission, if the blinds could be brought down. Your Honour, we may have a slight technical problem with the transcript. There's no transcript appearing, and the court reporter is indicating to me that in just a couple of minutes it should be working again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. We have to be patient. But the witness can come in in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. That would probably save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you order that the witness comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the technical problems are now sorted out, so we can continue and there will be a record of what we were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning. The witness has got a name, a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "R," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning. I won't call you by your name. I will ask you to take an oath, as the bailiff will indicate to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could just be shown his name just to confirm his identity, and I'll hand that to the Court's officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, show him the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, is your name written on the paper that was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And it will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness R.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, with your permission, if the blinds could be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. So it is not a full --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, it's not a closed session, Your Honour. The witness will have his face distorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So much the better, I hope, because I think some people are in the gallery, coming from some universities. Yes, here they are. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just wait one moment until the blinds are fully up and then I'll start my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness R, I shall call you Witness R so that your identity is protected. You're perfectly safe. Please relax as best you can. You're Bosnian by nationality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you're a Muslim by faith.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were a member of the Bosnian army until June or July of 1993, at which time you left as a result of injury; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, without naming the village to protect your identity, in July of 1995 you were living in a village in the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want you to cast your mind back to the 11th of July, to 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon on that day. You were in the village of Susnjari. Can you tell the Judge what you recall happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Simply, the enclave was captured by the Serbs, by the Serb army. I heard that it fell, that the town had fallen, simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We sent our families, women and children, to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. I felt that I was capable, as a younger man, that I shouldn't go, so I stayed behind so that more people would gather together and head to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you speak of more people gathering together to go to the woods, who were these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were people of Muslim ethnicity who were living in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they men or women or children, or a mixture of all three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Mostly men, and women. The children had left towards the UNPROFOR base in Potocari, and most of the women as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the age group of the men who gathered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: From 10 years old up to 60, even 70 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you had gathered, what did this group do, this group of what you described as mostly men from 10 to 60 or 70 years of age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: A kind of column was formed. Those are narrow paths so we knew we had to form lines. And we headed towards the woods, in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you in this column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Somewhere around the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On what date did you leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was the 12th, at about 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning when I set off from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you were armed. Can you describe to the Judge the weapon that you had with you and how much ammunition you had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There was a hunting rifle but not a proper rifle. It's a souvenir of my father, a single barrel, handmade rifle that was very old, maybe 100 years old. I had five or six bullets. Though the gun had never been used in battle and it wasn't a reliable one to shoot with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know you had an eventful journey through the woods, and the Defence indeed may have some questions for you about that, but I want to move ahead to the 13th of July and I want you to think about approximately the events that happened on the morning of the 13th of July, at 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning. First of all, I'd like to show you a map that you drew for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 159. Your Honour, this is a map which is computer generated. But the witness drew it for the Office of the Prosecutor on Sunday and he's, in fact, confirmed the route that he drew on this map matches the broken line that you see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, does this accurately reflect the route that you took from the Srebrenica enclave, ultimately arriving in Nezuk sometime after the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, that is the path.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could place that map onto the ELMO. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness R, could you point out to the Judge where you were located on the morning of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: [Inaudible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you say that again because I don't think the interpreters heard you. Could you speak up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was between Kasaba and Konjevic Polje, somewhere here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is identifying an area on the dotted line that lies directly between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba, so on a vertical line running through Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At what time were you at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Between 7.00 and 9.00, just then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You can take the pointer off that now. It's clear. Thank you. What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: A large group of people had congregated. In my estimate, I think there were 2.000, maybe even 3.000 people. It was morning, it had already dawned, and there was an open space without any woods to protect us. But the road had already been blocked, Kasaba-Konjevic Polje, by Serb units so that it was impossible to pass. We were there for about an hour or two, at least I was, and then I decided to move away from that spot into the surrounding woods about 500 metres away, and I stayed there the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the 2.000 people that you're speaking of, these were people that had left the Srebrenica enclave and had travelled in the column from the enclave, trying to escape to the free territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judge, while you were hiding in this wooded area, when you said you moved away to the surrounding woods, what you saw from your vantage point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: At about 1.00, I saw the Serb army surrounding this large group of people. Everyone separated from the group, 10, 20, or 30 metres, were killed by these troops; that is, they killed all those who were away from the group. However, most of the others were captured and forced towards the asphalt road leading from Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you're referring to the large group, this is the group of 2.000 people that you spoke of earlier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see anybody actually killed yourself on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was quite a number of people, only I wasn't right next to them to be able to recognise them or know their names. I was at a distance of 500, maybe 300 metres, as the crow flies, and I saw them killing these people, all of those who were around the group; whereas the group itself that was in one group, they were forced forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you recall how many people from the group you saw killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Quite a large number of people. In my opinion, between 200 and 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was doing the killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The Serb troops, the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you say that you were at a distance of between 300 and 500 metres from this shooting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's now move on to the 14th of July of 1995, and if you can tell the Judge what you did on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On that day, I took a roundabout route in the direction of Kasaba, and on the way I saw the tanks and APCs and Pragas and other weapons lined up. However, during the night, that is, on the 14th, early in the morning, we managed to cross over, about five or six of us -- actually, six to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you show Judge Riad on the map in front of you where it is you crossed the road. I think your route is marked across the road. The usher will put it onto the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could move it up a bit, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Here [indicates]. It was here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 159, that the witness is indicating that he crossed the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba at a point which is bisected by the dotted line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's move ahead in time to the 18th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that could be left on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher, and if you could move it down just a little bit. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate to Judge Riad the route that you took and the point at which you arrived, on the map, on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I took this route [indicates], and on the 18th of July we got here [indicates], we arrived here [indicates]. The place is called Bajkovica, as far as I knew, though I'm not too familiar with the parts. But some of the men who had already got there before us said that the place was called Bajkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 159, that he followed the broken line then to an area which is marked approximately by the shaded circle labeled "Bajkovica," and he states in his evidence that he arrived at that point on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many people reached Bajkovica on the 18th of July? How many from the group that had left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: These groups were moving in various directions so one cannot say that they arrived together. But at any event, when I got there, there were about 500 men already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you stay with this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, but very briefly, for an hour, because again we could hear shooting in the vicinity and we were called upon to surrender by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when you were called upon to surrender by the Serb army, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Again, knowing from experience what had happened between Konjevic Polje and Kravica, and fearing that I would be killed, again I decided, together with another group -- there were ten of us in all -- we split from that group and went into the woods again to pass around that road and avoid being with a large group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's move ahead in time again to the 19th of July of 1995, and if you can tell the Judge where you found yourself on that day, and in fact with how many other Bosnian Muslim men you were with on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. It is this place here [indicates] that has been marked on the map as Bajkovica, that has been shaded in and encircled in black. Together with ten other Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness, on the 19th of July, again was in and around an area which is marked approximately on the map as the area of Bajkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judge what happened to you and these other men on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was a tragic day. We were in a place where the Serb army had its front trenches, I think the first trenches at the beginning of the war, and we could see the Serb front line at a distance of a kilometre away from us, on a hill, in a wood. It was about 12.00, 12.30, when we were captured. We were on a small path next to these trenches. It was a freshly laid path and one could see that footsteps; I don't know whose they were. We took shelter in some bushes next to this small path, two or three metres away. We were tired, hungry. We sat down to have a rest. We were sitting there for some 15 minutes when we heard the Serb troops calling out that we should surrender. We couldn't see them because we were in the bushes, and if we were to get up they would be able to detect us. We hoped that we would manage to go unnoticed. However, not more than half an hour after their arrival, heavy shooting started above our heads. It went on for about ten minutes, and again they were shouting that we should surrender. And one of my comrades raised his hands. One by one we followed. I was the last one to do that. We came out to this path, which was only two or three metres away from us. I was the last in the group. I had a green shirt on. When I came out, there were two to three Serb soldiers on either side of the path that we took to reach them. We were slightly hit. However, I was hit the most because I had a green shirt, and I can show you the scars I still have here on my chin, and of course elsewhere too. I was beaten up the worst. We reached this path. They took us some 30 or 50 metres away and they told us to lie down on our stomachs, with our heads down and our hands stretched out. I then heard one Serb soldier saying, "Stari is coming," meaning the old man, "and he will tell us what to do." He can't have been far away, this Stari, maybe 50 or 100 metres away and he arrived very soon. He sat next to a tree and he asked, "Where is the rest of this army?" A soldier was carrying a radio transmitter, a Rup 12, which was next to this man they called Stari, and the soldier was sitting next to him, and they kept asking us where the other army was, the rest of the army. And one of us was saying that there were some close by, where the 500 men had stayed behind, and then Stari telephoned immediately, giving instructions. And I heard him saying to his soldiers, "The Vukovi," or the Wolves "will deal with that." Then he ordered us to give up all the documents or valuables and money that we had on us. We could only turn around to take out everything we had. Though I didn't surrender all my documents, most of the others did. And then the interrogations started one by one, asking us how many troops there were, what happened in Srebrenica, who the commanders were, and so on. The first thing that happened was that a young boy between 15 and 16, he was first asked how many men the brigade in Srebrenica had. The boy didn't know; he had not belonged to the army anyway because he was so young, as far as I know. And he said that there were between 30 to 50 men in a brigade. He ordered a soldier behind him, there was a Serb soldier standing behind each one of us with an automatic rifle pointed at our backs, and he ordered this soldier to take him away. He took this young boy to the right of us as we were lying there, at a distance of some four to six metres from us, and we just heard a single shot. I didn't hear a sound of a voice or anything. And the soldier came back. The second was again a boy who was already disabled. He was disabled from childhood, that is, he had two fingers missing on his left hand. And he was asked how he had lost those fingers. He told him the truth, that he had lost them as a child using an old hunting rifle, and that the rifle went off and took away his fingers, and that he wasn't a member of the army and I knew that he wasn't. He ordered that he should be taken away too. The soldier who was standing behind him with a gun pointed at him said, "I wouldn't like to do that now." I think he refused the commander's orders. The commander looked at him and said to another soldier that he should take him away, and that is what he did. He took him to the right, three metres away from us. Again we heard a single shot. I was the third. Stari said to me, why was I talking so much. He asked me where the army was and where it was moving. As I didn't know, I told him I didn't know where they are and where they are going to. I said there were men and they were on the move but I couldn't tell him exactly where they were. He immediately ordered this soldier behind me to take me off. As I was getting up, I felt awful so that I only just managed to get up. I took my time. And he asked me, "What's wrong? Why aren't you getting up?" I looked at him because he was the one who had beat me the most and he knew very well what was wrong. But I managed to get up, nevertheless, and when I did I saw this other man who had been shot, who was lying on his side, and I could see that he was dead by the colour of his skin. As the ground was uneven, there was a slope there where they were sitting and we were lying on this small path, I headed towards this comrade who was already dead, so I went slightly down the slope. I turned my head and looked at the soldier cocking his trigger, with his automatic rifle pointed at me. The distance between him and me was one metre, and when he stretches out his arm it couldn't have been more than half a metre. He fired the shot which hit me here [indicates]. I can show the doctor's certificate of where the shot hit me in my left shoulder. I was waiting to die, but I still felt quite well, and I thought that I would die a little later. However, I survived. It was very hard to live through this. A Serb soldier, after I fell to the ground, sat down some two or one and a half metres away from me, so I could see a part of his boots. He was sitting there smoking and looking at me. I couldn't breathe because he might notice and repeat the shot. The worst part was that I was bleeding all over, and when I was beaten, there was blood coming out my mouth and nose and ears, so the ants were attracted by the blood and I had to keep my mouth open to be able to breathe, and these ants were coming into my mouth and I could hardly endure it. However, I managed until late into the night. It was already dark when they left this spot. While I was lying there, another man was taken out. I could feel it and not see it because he passed by me, led by this soldier, to a spot three or four metres away from me. And the same scene repeated itself: one shot and he fell. I could hear him breathing his last sigh of life. And lying there, I could hear more of these shots, more of these comments. Stari pointing at us, having probably captured some other soldiers, he was saying, "See how your soldiers have fared lying there in the woods?" And that is the end of that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just have a number of questions to clarify what you've said. Now, you spoke in your testimony about a man called Stari. How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they called him, Stari. He had a military uniform on, without any insignia or rank, and it was a camouflage army uniform. He was somewhat older, he was bald, he had hairy arms, short in build. That's what he looked like, what I was able to notice at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence that the soldiers looked to Stari for instructions. Did Stari appear to be in charge on the ground at this spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Stari was in charge there. That was obvious. You could notice that quite evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that you saw another soldier with a radio transmitter; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was a soldier with a radio transmitter, a Rup 12. I knew this because I had done my military service in the former Yugoslav People's Army and I could recognise this type of radio transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you saw, I think, Stari on the radio passing instructions to another unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And those instructions, I think you said in your evidence, concerned the other group of 500 Muslim men who were still in the woods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's how it was. One of them explained that the group was there and he gave strict orders that the group should be finished off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And again, just for absolute clarity, you're talking about the other group of 500 Muslim men in the woods. That's the group that he said should be finished off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No. The group at Baljkovica, where I arrived on the 18th. There wasn't another group in the woods. There were the ten of us there who had left on the 18th, and on the 19th we gathered at that place where we were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when he said, "Finish them off," who is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, that group. That group was there where we explained it was. And as the group was there, you could notice some voices, some people were groaning who were not able to go further away. Quite simply, they didn't know where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how many were in that group? How many men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: About 500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken to be shot yourself, you only saw one other dead man; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you stated in your evidence how two men had been taken away to be shot before you. Where was the other man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken to the left, the other one was taken to the right. So that -- the fern was fairly high so you couldn't see properly, that is to say, I didn't even have time to look, to look at that first one, the first one that was shot, that young boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, while you were lying there after you had been shot, how many further shots did you hear; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were a number of shots. One, two or three minutes after me, as far as I was able to assess, although it was a very difficult moment for me and I can't give you a time span. But very shortly after me, one was taken off; I'm certain of that. But several shots were heard. Now, I don't know whether they took them off to the right-hand side, perhaps where that first young boy had been shot, or perhaps they had taken them off further from me, that they were not as close to me. And I couldn't see anything at that moment because, as I said, my head was facing downwards, into the ground, and I couldn't see anything. All I could do was hear things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's go back to uniforms again. I realise these were very difficult moments for you. Do you recall on any of these Serb soldiers, on any of these 50 soldiers, seeing any badges on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, there were some signs, insignia. On the left-hand arm, as far as I was able to notice, although as I say, this was a very short space of time and it was all very difficult for me to see. I had my head down on the ground, to the left. But on the left-hand arm there was a yellow insignia. Perhaps there was some other colour there but it was predominantly yellow, and there was a yellow sort of circle and it said "The Krajisnici," men from Krajisnici, something like that, on this circle in this patch. It was difficult to make it out because he moved his arm around so I couldn't actually see. But I'm certain of that. And that was the patch that most of the soldiers had on them. But I think, that is to say, I'm quite sure, actually that it said "Drinski" on some of the patches as well. I just saw the "Drinski", the word "Drinski". What the "Drinski" was after what the other word was, I couldn't see. I couldn't see the whole of this circle on the patch, just the "Drinski" part. As far as the Krajisnik or Krajisnici are concerned, I'm 100 per cent certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said later into the evening the Bosnian Serb soldiers left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you do after they'd left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I'd been lying there for quite some time, and when I was sure that there were no more noises, and nobody around, and it was already dark, I raised my head a little to see if there was anybody about anywhere, just to make sure, but I didn't hear anybody. So I raised my head and I found it very difficult to get up because I had become rigid from all that lying down. But I did manage to raise myself a little and sit down, and I saw that there was nobody anywhere around. I called out two or three times, "Is there anybody alive" in a quiet voice but nobody responded to my call. One of the people lying next to me, I was able -- I looked to see if he was alive, but he gave no signs of life, he was already dead. I touched him to see. But I didn't have the strength to examine the others, to see what had happened to them, as I was in the woods and it was dark. But I did manage to see that he was dead, and I carried on towards free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just indicate to Judge Riad on the map next to you the route that you took from Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was this direction here [indicates], with the dotted line. The dotted line shows the route towards Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is showing, on Exhibit 159, a route leading from an area shaded Baljkovica, across the confrontation line to the town or village of Nezuk. Now, if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 151, and this shouldn't go on the ELMO because it identifies the witness. And if he could be shown 151A which is the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, this is a letter of discharge from the war hospital and it essentially describes the injury to your left shoulder. Can you just confirm, for our record, that these in fact are your medical records.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, they are my medical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, the English translation is Exhibit 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just have a few more questions for you. I'm not going to show you this statement, but this is a statement -- although in fact the Defence may wish to, but this is a statement that you gave to the Bosnian authorities on the 26th of August of 1995, and you and I have already discussed this. You state, and I'll read slowly for the purposes of the record, at the beginning of that statement: "I was together with the majority of the inhabitants on the defence lines in the area of Susnjari and Jaglici." And this is referring to early July. Now, you will recall in your evidence you stated that you had left the Bosnian army in June or July of 1993. Were you on the defence lines in July of 1995, or is that statement incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I was not on the defence lines at that time, in 1995, in June, because, as I've already said, I left in June/July 1993, I left that army; that is to say, it wasn't actually an army in my opinion, even up until then, it was the Territorial Defence, in fact. And with the proclamation of the demilitarised zones there was no army in Srebrenica because the weapons had been taken away from the overall Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I just have a couple more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, if we could go into closed session because I want to ask him about one of the survivors, and if he starts naming individuals who are executed and the survivors, he will identify himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: For how long, do you think, for the gallery?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: A couple of minutes. Thank you. You can draw the curtains.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The curtains don't need to go down. We can have a private session, just so that the public feed is cut for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We don't need to draw the curtains.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've said that the execution took place on the 19th of July, and I know this is not a time that you were inspecting your watch regularly, but do you recall approximately what time these executions took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think it was about 12.30. From 12.00 to 1.00 in the afternoon, in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many of your male relatives did you lose during Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Many. I lost many members of my family. My brother, my father, and a lot of other family members, practically all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you one of the few male members of your extended family still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, I have no further questions of the witness, so I can offer him for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Would you rather have a break now before the cross-examination starts? Who will assume the cross-examination, Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Witness R's cross-examination will be done by me. I am counsel Petrusic. And we agree with your proposal to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Then I'll ask the witness to have a rest and to come back. You know the procedure here is that you will be asked questions by the Defence counsel, who will help finding out the truth which we are all searching for here. So we will adjourn for half an hour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, would you proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness R, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put some questions to you in keeping with the procedure, and I shall try not to have to take you back to everything that you lived through.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My first question, Witness R, is who told you that you had to leave the Susnjari area on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: From two men, two men I don't know, who passed through the region and explained to the people that the women and children should be sent towards the UNPROFOR base in Potocari, that is to say, and anybody else who wanted to, and the ones who didn't want to, that they should gather in one spot and take to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were they soldiers, members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: For the most part they were not soldiers. And in fact at that time there was no army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What did exist was the Territorial Defence, until the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. So with the gathering of these people, there were those who were, perhaps, in uniform but they came by the uniforms in their own way, they got them themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, these two individuals, my question is directed towards them, were they wearing uniforms, military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, you gave a statement to the State Security Service of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 26th of August, 1995; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to have this statement shown to the witness and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will handle that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For you to be able to follow, I have marked the passages on page 1 that I'm going to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, this statement, that is to say, the signature at the end of it, is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is it your statement, therefore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think it is. I didn't read through the whole of it, but looking at the signatures, they are mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, my learned colleague Mr. Cayley indicated a portion of this statement, read it out, and I should like to say that in the first sentence you state the following, after the first sentence which ends with "Zeleni Jadar," you go on to say: "I was together with the majority of the inhabitants on the defence lines in the region of Susnjari and Jaglici." Did you, in fact, state that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That I was in the vicinity of Susnjari and Jaglici, yes, but that I was at the lines, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Further on you say that: "At around 1800 hours, on the 11th of July, 1995, after the breakdown of the defences of Srebrenica, two soldiers unknown to me came to Susnjari and told the people that women, children, and the elderly should retreat to the UN base in Potocari, while the men of fighting age were, with the other civilians, to try to break through the enemy lines and reach the free territory with the remaining citizens." Did you tell that to the State Security Service on the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that the two soldiers were there, and that I said that we went towards this breakthrough, I did not -- to try to break through, I did not use the word "breakthrough," "proboj," in respect of the army and weapons. I think that most probably, according to the stories, how it was recounted, they drew up this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But you did sign the document nonetheless, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign it. However, as I was not confronted with the giving of -- I had never given statements before this case, I cannot agree. I don't agree that I said all this in this particular way and that every word is as I said it and that it means something. I am not a lawyer myself, and what I did was recount the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the people who took down your statement were qualified, educated, and trained to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the people who took the statement down, I just met them; that is to say, they found me and they called me to give a statement. They just introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that they forged your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, judging by this, perhaps they added some words of their own to it. That is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, as far as you are aware, how many able-bodied men gathered in Jaglici or Susnjari on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact figure because I didn't count them, but it was a very large group of people. But they were not all of military age. There were some from 10 up to 60, and even 70 years of age, and they were mostly civilians, civilian persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You had a hunting rifle, an old hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, with one barrel, handmade, as a souvenir from my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that possibly some other members in the group had similar weapons, hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of such weapons, but not a large number; a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was any military, so-called military weapons left over, automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs, semi-automatic rifles, the kind of weapons used by the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were some but very, very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, did you hear from your fellow citizens when you crossed into free territory, did you hear anything in connection with the part of the column that was armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I heard about a part of that column that crossed over, a very, very small number of people, that they were assisted by the BiH army at the crossing at Baljkovica to pull out. A certain number, how many, I don't know, I didn't see them, but they didn't really have any weapons. At the beginning they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So when the column was formed, they didn't have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They did have weapons but not real weapons. They had some hunting rifles and some Kalashnikovs, automatic rifles. They had something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As you were going from Susnjari, Jaglici, to Buljim and descending towards the Konjevic Polje-Kasaba road, was there any exchange of fire within the group you were moving with, within the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: At one point, near the village of Kamenica, this large group congregated and we were surrounded, and there were shots fired from all sides. I cannot say that I saw shooting or fire exchanged within the group, because of course one cannot hit one's own when everyone is seeking salvation. But there was shooting and you couldn't really tell. It was coming from all sides, and anyway, we were totally encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about possibly suicides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were several killings in a large group between Konjevic Polje and Kasaba. In this large group, several wounded persons killed themselves, and I saw that. They simply couldn't go any further. They were lying down, they put grenades under their bodies and committed suicide. They had no other choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were living in a locality close to Srebrenica which was part of the demilitarised zone. Tell me, please, did you ever hear about the existence of a military formation called the 28th Division, under the command of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did know of the 28th Division, everyone knows that, but it was the Territorial Defence and that was at the beginning. Simply, everyone defended his own village until Srebrenica was demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So after the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, there was no 28th Division, nor Naser Oric there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I'm not saying that they weren't there. Naser was there; I saw him. But as for the army, it was not there. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Naser was the commander of a unit without troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I don't know how I can answer that question. If there are no troops, how can he be a commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But you said that you saw Naser and that he was a commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I saw him as a person. I couldn't see him as a commander. I don't know how I can say he was a commander. You can tell me someone here is a commander, but how can I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On three occasions since 1995 to the present, you gave statements to the Ministry of the Interior, to the State Security Service, and to the team of investigators of the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did give those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This was in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your recollections in August 1995 regarding those events -- and you must understand me, please, I do not wish to insist on the horrors that you experienced -- but I have to say that your recollections then were surely fresher than they are today. This is a biological fact, I might say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: One might say that I am in a more focused state of mind now than then. It was fresher, more recent, but the concentration, after a time has gone by, can improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, today you are telling us about an event involving a large number of people, a very significant event, when, according to you, about 200 people were executed in Konjevic Polje, close to the group which numbered about 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were not people who were executed, lined up and executed. Some people were sitting; some were standing. But all those who were separate from this large group, who were some distance away from the group were simply killed because they were surrounded on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't use the right expression. But according to your testimony, 200 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, the number is between 200 and 300. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, Witness R, the fact that never in any of your previous statements, and there was this professional team of investigators interviewing you which, in the opinion of the Defence, could not have allowed themselves the luxury of leaving out such an important event, was never mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. In every statement they kept cautioning me that it wasn't important that -- that it was important to say only what I actually saw. If I was a little further away, that wasn't important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You were cautioned to that effect by the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that I should recount the things that happened to me, whereas other people would tell about other experiences. .

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Further in your statement, one notes that you mention for the first time today units that you describe as Drinski.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. I mostly spoke about the Krajisnici, Krajiska. But in thinking over what actually happened, I could see one letter, like "D", like "Drina", like "Drinski". So in my opinion, there were soldiers with such insignia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned a single letter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, one letter. It was on the left sleeve, and they always faced us or were behind us. My head was bent, looking at the ground, so I couldn't turn around to read whatever it said. So we could see very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But you saw the letter "D"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, "Drinski". Maybe I wasn't able to decipher each and every letter, but "Dre" and then one naturally concludes that it must be "Drinski".

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, the investigators that interviewed you in August certainly asked you about units, because you mentioned Krajisnici and such like. Can you explain then, as this happened to you, why did you not mention then the unit that was wearing this emblem with the word "Drinski" or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I just explained a moment ago that thinking back to that event, I was reminded that I saw "Drinski" on a few of those soldiers. Not all. Most of them were "Krajiska", "Krajisnici", most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In what alphabet was that written?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I studied Latin and Cyrillic scripts, there was no Cyrillic, as far as one could remember. But this was a very difficult moment when you can't notice or hear or register everything. It is hard to imagine, and it is hard to be certain at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I quite understand. But as far as I'm able to understand from what you just said, both scripts were represented, the Cyrillic and the Latin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, since "K" is written in the same way in both scripts, the letter "K" was there. And since the letter "R" has only one more line, it is "P" in the Latin script and "R" in the Cyrillic script, the two are similar again. And I studied both scripts at school, so it's not so confusing to me. I can read both. But as far as I can remember, it was in Cyrillic script, but it's quite possible that it might have been in Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure it said "Krajisnici", "Krajiska", or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness R, I'm asking you about Drinski.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, that's a different question. You asked me about the Krajisnici. As for Drinski -- I don't know how I can explain this to you. Everything I have said about Krajisnici also applies to Drinski. I studied the Latin and Cyrillic scripts, and that is how I deciphered the patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So my question is: Are you sure that it was one or the other script or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I'm sure that it said "Krajisnici". And thinking things over well, I have a feeling that there was "Drinski" too. This is a feeling. But "Krajisnici", "Krajiska", that I'm sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So regarding "Drinski", you have a feeling that it was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. As to what I feel now and remember now, I must underline once again that these were difficult moments, and in such moments it is difficult to expect a lot, because just imagine if you were in such a situation, how you would feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To wind up this cross-examination, when you crossed over to free territory, did you learn from your friends and acquaintances, who had also crossed into that territory, anything about who had crossed the Rajkovici mountain, the confrontation line there, that an agreement had been made between the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and the commander who led that group; in other words, that an agreement had been reached to open the lines at Bajkovac and to allow the convoy to pass?. This was on the 17th or the 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I sorry, I didn't hear that, but I know that they went through similar troubles with the assistance of the BiH army that somehow managed to deblock the area to help this group pull out. That is what I heard. But that there was an agreement, I didn't hear anything about it; nor did I see the Serb army allowing anyone to pass, nor did I hear about any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions. Witness R, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Cayley, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness R, I would like to just clarify a few points which you mentioned. When you spoke of what Mr. Cayley called a vantage point in the woods -- I don't know how they translated that in Serbo-Croat because "vantage point" is a very sophisticated word -- I think you saw between 200 or 300 people killed by the Serb troops. Were they killed in the fighting or was it a summary execution? Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. It wasn't in fighting, it was killing people at random, people who were standing there, who had decided to surrender to the Serb army because they didn't know where to go. And they were waiting for the Serb army to approach them, and as they approached them, the Serb troops, they killed those around. I assume they killed them. Anyway, I saw people falling to the ground and being shot at. What actually happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You saw that very clearly from where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You saw the shooting or you saw the bodies on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I saw the bodies, and I saw a man, as he was hit, falling down. Some people crying out, screaming out, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you saw the whole event and not the aftermath, just people lying down. You saw and heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. It was from the nearby woods. It wasn't far away, as the crow flies. If we were to measure this distance, it would be 300 to 500 metres away. And as we were on the hill and they were down in the vale, one could see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Very good. Now, when you spoke about this old man, Stari, among other things which you said, he said, "The Wolves will deal with them," if you remember what you said. What did you conclude from that? What is the meaning of "Wolves" and what is the meaning of "deal with them", if you can put that in the context you are in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The Wolves, I think, were -- as I could hear from others, that they were a unit, a Serb unit. And when he said they would deal with them, what I thought he meant was that they would catch them and do something. I don't know what. Probably what he did with us. That was my idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What they did with you, it means shooting or killing, what you said about yourself. That was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, speaking of you, you were shot at a distance of one metre, and you were lying down on the ground in your blood until night. Now, were you in shape to move after that? Did you have the strength to start moving after that? What happened exactly? Did somebody carry you or were you able to go through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There was no one there to help me. I managed to get up. It was hard. I was all stiff. But by budging left and right, I managed to sit up. And after sitting for five to ten minutes, I somehow managed to climb up against a tree to get on my feet. As I was wounded in the shoulder, I could walk. I hadn't lost so much blood as not to be able to walk. I could walk with difficulty but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Very good. Just with reference to the insignia you thought you saw, the Drinski insignia, you said you had the feeling that this insignia existed. Can you just explain how this feeling came to you? What gave you this feeling? You heard people mentioning the word or you read it? If you can try to know the origin of this feeling, if you could.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult because this Stari who was giving orders said, "The Wolves will deal with it," and I thought he meant the Drina Wolves because I had heard of that unit. As for Krajisnici or Krajiska, I am sure of this emblem. It is a yellow-coloured patch on the left sleeve worn by all these soldiers. But when I think hard, I have a feeling that there were soldiers who were also wearing similar patches with the word "Drinski." But I have this feeling now after a long period of time and after thinking hard. For Krajiski, Krajisnici, or Krajiska, I am sure of that. It was a yellow patch, and I can show you this patch. If you can get a hold of an example of this patch, I'm sure I would be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The Krajisnici. You are concentrating on the Krajisnici badge; is that right? This is the thing you are sure of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. There are three possibilities; Krajisnici, Krajiska, or something to that effect. I think it said "Krajiska," "Krajisnici," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And did you have an idea of where these people would come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you hear them speak? Did you hear their dialect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, the dialect amongst the Serbs, at least, is similar, so I can't judge by their speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you don't know whether they were coming from Serbia, from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's all the questions I wanted to ask you. I would like to thank you very much for coming and congratulate you for getting out of this great ordeal alive and safe and sound. Thank you very much. Mr. Bailiff, we'll have to take him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, before the witness leaves, we have a number of exhibits that need to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Before he leaves. Then before he leaves, I would like to ask him if he would like to add anything to what he said. Anything you would like to mention, to tell the Tribunal? You have come the whole way, and you are entitled to be heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was my only wish, to have the opportunity to tell about what happened to normal people so that they can feel and see what they did, so that they can remember what they did. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness R. I can't say your name. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of exhibits, and I think my learned friend has one exhibit too. First of all, Exhibit 151, which is an English translation of a letter of discharge and medical report, and Exhibit 151A, which is the original of that report in the Bosnian language. I would apply for formal admission into evidence of those two documents. They should remain under seal because they identify the witness. The second item is Exhibit 159, which is the map which the witness originally drew a trace, which we then incorporated into a computer-generated image of what he drew us. That document does not need to be under seal. And then lastly, if the private session -- where he gave evidence in private session could remain under seal, because he does identify an individual in that part of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Does the Defence have any document to present into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no objection regarding the documents tendered by the Prosecutor. And I think D19 is the exhibit shown to Your Honours which we would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can add in respect of D19, and I'm sure my learned friend won't object, it should be under seal because the document identifies the witness. It has his signature and name upon it, so it should remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think we have to keep it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness R, we'll ask you to leave, and thank you again. We better draw the shutters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think so. Judge Riad, while this is taking place, Mr. McCloskey and I will change places because he's leading the next witness, unless you wish to take a short break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, we can continue. Perhaps you can ask him if he wants to lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness S, you are a Bosnian by nationality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And a Muslim by faith.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were living in July of 1995 and who you were living with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I lived in Srebrenica with my family, my wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And on July 11th, did you decide to do something along with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 11th of July we had to separate. I decided to go with the other men, to take to the woods, and my wife and children remained and went with the other people to the UNPROFOR base at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the circumstances why you decided you had to leave your home and your family had to leave their home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I saw that the situation was a chaotic one, a terrible one, and there was no other way out. We could only expect death down there because we had no protection from UNPROFOR, and we decided to take to the woods.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is that because the Serb army had taken over Srebrenica on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, it had already taken over half the town, from the hill of Bojna. And there was no reason to wait any longer, there was no possibility for safety.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Your family went to Potocari, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I went with all the other men towards the village of Slatine and Susnjari, upwards.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: About how many other men were gathered in the area of Susnjari when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, there were about 12.000 and 15.000. I can't give you an exact figure, but there were a lot of us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many of those men might have been armed in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: As far as I was able to note, about a third, I'd say, with hunting rifles, not very strong weaponry; hunting rifles and other types. But a third of them, I would say. Not more.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, have some kind of armament?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you have some military explosive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In my bag I had a hand grenade which I put there, if I were captured by the Serbs, to be able to take my own life.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you set off -- what time did you set off from Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, from a field in front of a house, I left there at around noon, between 12.00 and 1.00, towards the Bojna hill.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was that the evening of the 11th, or was it noon on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was in the evening of the 12th -- no, I'm sorry. It was between the 11th and 12th. We started out on the 11th, at about 2.30, and in the evening we arrived at Susnjari at about 10.00. We had a consultation there. So that at about 12.00, midnight, that is to say, we started out. The night between the 11th and 12th.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was this consultation you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, we lined up so that as many people could cross as possible, because the Serb lines were very near and there were a lot of us. Around Causi and the surrounding hills, that's where they were.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was someone leading the consultation or leading this large group of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No. They just tried to line us up so that people with weapons and without weapons would be mixed up together, and if we came across an ambush, to prevent as many people losing their lives as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you say "they," -- so there were some people leading this, or trying to communicate to the large group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, there was the head of the municipality, those in charge of civilian authority, and some others who were in Srebrenica in the course of the war, the chiefs of some secretariats for example.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you notice military people too that had been in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, there was the Territorial Defence. It wasn't an army, because it was a demilitarised zone, so there was just this sort of Territorial Defence if the situation would arise, as it in fact did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So there were some Territorial Defence people there also.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I know you spent some time through the woods, but I'm going to -- the counsel for the Defence may ask you about that, the Judge, but I would like also, I'd like to take you, if I could, through the 12th and start out with the late evening hours of the 12th. If you could tell us where you were on the late hours of the 12th and what you recall happening then, and then work your way onto the morning of the 13th when you were captured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 12th, at 11.30, I crossed the first Serb lines. At about 2.00, 2.30, there was an ambush towards the village of Kamenica --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mean 11.30 a.m. and then 2.30 p.m. on the 12th there was an ambush?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, at noon on the 12th, because I was at Buljim, in front of the first Serb lines from the morning, from 5.00 a.m. until 11.30. We were not able to cross over, and the column was interrupted. And at 11.30, I crossed the first Serb line with a group and then we came across an ambush by a stream. And sometime in the afternoon I reached the Kamenica Hill, where I saw a lot of soldiers who had gone ahead. The situation was one of chaos. First of all, they said that the wounded should go in front, and I took a wounded man and went in front. But towards evening we went to the village of Kamenica and moved on towards the village of Unice [phoen]. As we were going down from the village of Kamenica I drank a lot of water, and by 12.00 we went up through the village of Burnice. I felt very sleepy and I don't know what time it was, 12.00, 12.30, and I lost consciousness. I woke up in the morning at around 3.00 a.m. and got to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So this is the morning of the 13th that you got to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness what is marked as Exhibit 176, and could that be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I believe you've told us previously that you were near the intersection at Konjevic Polje. Could you point out just roughly where you found yourself the morning of the 13th. You can just point with your finger on that map. No, you've got the pointer. That's great.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I found myself by the road, between Kravica Rijeka and the road towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you use the pointer and show us what you mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It is this section here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That's the -- you're pointing to the intersection just, it looks like, perhaps a kilometre south of the little dot that says "Konjevic Polje." Can you describe the situation you found yourself in that morning. What occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When I came to, regained consciousness, I looked at my watch and it was about 3.00 a.m. I was in some grassland and then went into a cornfield of some kind. And I saw that I was in a very grave situation. As I knew the terrain slightly from before the war, I saw a bridge which goes towards Kasaba. I thought about what I was going to do next, and I went down towards the river, which flows from the Kravica direction and it flows under the bridge and joins up with the Jadar River. But I thought that the river was enormous, it looked enormous to me, and then when I looked down to the River Jadar from the bridge it seemed even larger and I thought that it would take me off. So I went back to the field, that cornfield actually, and I sat down there. There was a burnt-down house there. In front of it there was a slightly newer house which had not been burnt to the ground. And I took some tobacco out of my pocket and wanted to roll a cigarette to make myself feel better. But when I got the tobacco out, I put it on my knee, rested it on the knee of my leg, and I just couldn't get my fingers together to roll up a cigarette, I felt so awful. And I shook my head to see if that would help me regain consciousness fully and to feel better, but it didn't. And then I heard that there were some people close by, and I tried to go into a house which had been partially burnt down. At the entrance to that house, at the stairway, I stepped on a brick, that is to say, a tile from the roof, and it snapped. And the people saw me and started shouting at me. They said, "Surrender. We can see you." And they shot up in the air above me and I put my hands up, put my bag up on my shoulder. They told me to approach, towards the asphalt road, which led from the intersection to Bratunac. I came up to these group of men, and they said, "Put your hands up," and I raised my hands even higher. They asked what I had in my bag. "Do you have any weapons?" I said I did not, and they told me ...

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, as you know, what you're saying has to be interpreted. I can tell that you're going a little -- if you can just slow down a little bit and just tell us the main things that occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: At that moment the first policeman came up to me, he took my bag away, took out the hand grenade which was in the bag and which I had intended to commit suicide with. He asked me what I had in my pockets. Then he searched my pockets and took out the tobacco, he took out my lighter from my pocket and wallet, in which I had 310 German marks. I had my passport, my ID card, my diary and telephone directory with the telephone numbers of my family abroad, and I had a ticket.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he take --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Which I had for work --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So he took all those identification documents. That's the first thing -- that's one of the first things that this person you've described as a police officer took; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, can you describe what this person you've described as a police officer was wearing, and what the other people that he was with were wearing who captured you that morning at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were several of them there. They were standing five to ten metres away. They had dark blue uniforms and slightly multicoloured. They weren't all blue, they were the mass type of blue uniform and they were all in one. They had a belt around their waist in front.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you notice any insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After they took all your ID documents, what happened? And tell us when you come to a point where you were able to recognise someone so we can stop.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That other policeman, the second one who was standing next to the one that had taken my documents from me, he said, "Lie down so I can slit your throat." I laid down by the roadside and said, "Go ahead. Slit my throat. Go ahead." But a third person was there and he said, "Don't touch him. Leave him alone," and he told me to get up. I got up, and he said to the other one, "Take him up there." And he took me off towards a school building. And in the meantime, while they were shooting at me, a civilian jumped out of the grass, he threw a grenade. He was on half of this asphalt road. He was of medium height. He had a check jacket on and his face was covered in blood. They shouted at me and said, "Is that your brother?" And I said no, it's not. They asked me whether I knew him, and I said I didn't. And he said that I should pull him off the asphalt road, onto the bank, the grassy bank by the side. I took him by the legs and pulled him over.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, what exactly did this person do with the grenade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think that he had this grenade and he threw it, and he killed himself on that road.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: With the grenade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And that happened before you were captured or after you were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think while they were shooting at me, he must have been close by, some 50 metres away. I didn't notice him, but I found him there dead.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let's get on with your testimony. You said that you were taken to a place near a school. Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can we just dwell on this man with the grenade? Did he throw it on himself to commit suicide, or did he throw it at the people shooting at Witness S?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Just to try to confirm that, did the person with the grenade use that grenade to kill himself, or did he throw it at the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think that he tried to run across the road. I was a little further away so I didn't quite see it. And he had no other way.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know if the explosion of the hand grenade killed him or whether Serb bullets killed him, or could you tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: His face was covered in blood and he had a jacket on him. I couldn't see any other wounds. And he was lying face down, with his arms spread out on the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see the hand grenade explode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No. It was fear, probably. There were five or six of them, they were shooting over me from automatic rifles. I was scared so I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see him throw the hand grenade away from himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No. He may have been some 40 metres away from me, so I didn't see him. I just saw him dead.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Why did you think there was a hand grenade involved in his death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That's what they told me, and the blood was still hot. When I picked him up first by the arms, and then the legs, my arms were bloody and his blood was warm, so it was a fresh wound.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay. It's important that when you're testifying, just testify about what you saw and heard, and if someone -- if you're testifying about what someone else told you, make sure you tell us that also, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were first taken by these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They took me to an area in front of the school. There was a like a small shed. And there were a couple of soldiers in camouflage uniforms in that shed. There were two other men that I knew. There were traces of blows on them. The man brought me there, a man I knew, and he told them, "Don't anyone touch him." But they tried to enter, there was one with a rifle there who was watching over us, they wanted to come in and beat us and they said, "Look at him, how big he is." Afterwards a man came talking to me, asking me where I had worked, what I did, where I was during the war, did I have money, had they taken the money from me, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we've reached the point where he recognises some people, so we should go into private session, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
