utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, please order a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Exhibit 177. And could you put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you recognise the little building depicted in 177?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were taken in relation to that building, and show us with your pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He took me along this path [indicates], and then I entered the house from this side [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, he shows that he entered this little brick building, in the forefront of the photo, from what would be the right side.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've already testified that there were at least two Muslim men you knew in there that were captives, and a Serb policeman that you knew. What occurred in the building, and where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The Serb policeman brought me there, and apart from us -- next to us were soldiers in camouflage uniforms, and he disappeared. He later came again and told us that we had to go somewhere for some officers to question us. And then he led us from this small building forward, along this path, across a meadow, to another house.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, the person that led you to another house, was that a Serb policeman that you had known earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And he wasn't the one you just saw very briefly and then disappeared, he was the one who you saw for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In fact, this one Serb policeman was with you most of the time in Konjevic Polje, until you were given to the execution squad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. So you were -- where did you go from that little brick building in the last exhibit? Where did this policeman take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We crossed a meadow, towards the crossroads. I don't know how many metres away exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When we got in front of this house, we found there four men in uniform who were sitting around a table lengthwise, and there was another table at right angles and we stood next to that table. To my left was the policeman I knew, and to my right were another two policemen whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 178, and could we put that on the ELMO. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I suggest that in five minutes we have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And we will resume at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry to the interpreters. Mr. McCloskey, I suggest that in five minutes we have a break and we'll resume at a quarter past one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Petrusic, can we continue until 2.15?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, Mr. President. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you point with the pointer again to the house where you were taken to the outside, where these men were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Next to this big building [indicates], in front of this tree [indicates].

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember those trees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've always told us that you remember those two apple trees. Are those the two apple trees that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, can you describe the men that questioned you, how many there were and what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was sitting at the head of the table, and the other three to the side. And the one sitting at the head questioned us most. When they lined us up in front of this other table, he said, "Don't lie. We know everything." And then he asked me where I was, what I was, where I worked. I answered some questions, and he said that he didn't believe me. Then he went on to the man next to me, and then on to the third man. The officers who were sitting around the table had a bottle of liquor in front of them and four small glasses, and they were drinking this alcoholic beverage. Then they questioned us in some detail. They told us about certain things, whether we had heard about them, some operations, offensive operations against Srebrenica. I said no. And then later they asked us whether we were hungry. We said we were. And from a wooden hut they brought us two small loaves of bread and some salami. We started eating. We took a little. We didn't have much strength. And they encouraged us, "Why aren't you eating?" And we said we couldn't. And they said, "Are you thirsty," and we said we were. And then he ordered one of the policemen to bring us water. He went into the house and brought us water. We drank. In the meantime, while they were still questioning us and we were answering, along the asphalt road from Bratunac, 12 buses came with women and children on board, and they told us to leave the food and to turn around and face the road, which we did. After that they asked us, "Did you see that?" We said yes. Then they said, "Turn around." And then he said, "You see how respectful they were of us, that they didn't force too many people onto the buses but only as many as could sit down." And I said, "Yes, you're good." And after a short while this policeman came up, the one who was sitting at the head of the table. I must not mention his name yet. He said, "Take them down there." And then this policeman took us into this house, in front of this house, and when we entered that house --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Before we get to this new policeman that you -- you know at least this policeman's first name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It is the same one who took me to the small house and brought me from that small house to the people who were interrogating me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So it's the same guy that you've been talking about all along?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some more particular questions about the person that you said was sitting at this table that first asked you questions. Can you describe what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform. His sleeves were turned up. He had a moustache. And the other one, or rather the third one at the end of the table was grey-haired --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let's just stay with this one guy first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The first one with the moustache, what colour uniform was he wearing, camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was the colour of camouflage uniforms worn by their officers.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: It wasn't blue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, no. No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: It was a regular soldier's camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. All four were wearing this military camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All four of the men that were at this table, that were participating in the interrogation, were all in military camouflage uniform, not blue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. But the one at the head of the table put most questions, and the one at the end. The other two kept quiet. They just looked at us; they didn't ask us much.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay. The person at the head of the table, he had a moustache; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What did he tell you about himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He told us that he had been in command of the operation on Srebrenica in 1993, in the area of Kade Voda and Osmace. And he told us how many shells they fired. They expected to find thousands dead, but they only found four soldiers dead in a bunker.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he tell you his nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us his nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "You have heard on the Motorola the name Cica. That was me."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said there was a grey-haired man at the other end of the table. Can you describe that person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was a little taller than this one. He was a little plumper. And I just remember the way he looked at us, as he was closest to us. He had grey hair. He was maybe over 50, a couple of years over 50, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: About how tall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was sitting down. Once they got up very briefly -- actually, these two in the middle were saying that General Mladic was coming, so we didn't dare turn around. They jumped up. The one at the head of the table said that it wasn't General Mladic; it wasn't his car. And then he said, "You've had it if Mladic comes." And then they looked, and then they sat down again, saying it wasn't Mladic. We didn't turn around, so we didn't see what colour the car was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How tall was, your best guess, the grey-haired fellow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, maybe 170, 180 centimetres. He was quite heavy. In his 50s; 55 maybe, in that age group.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question before we break. About what time did this occur, where these people were interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: About -- between 7.00 and 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour. This may be a good time to break, on your recommendation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We'll resume at twenty past one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just noticed the defendant coming in.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness S, we had just left off and you were about to be taken from the place where you'd been interrogated by four people in camouflage army uniforms, and you were being taken by the police officer that you'd known. Where did he take you this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, there's a detail that I forgot to tell you. While I was being interrogated, they asked us whether we drank alcoholic beverage and I said we did, and he said to another policeman to bring us a glass. Then he poured some alcohol from the bottle. I took the glass first and swallowed the alcohol, but I felt a sort of shock going through me. I passed the glass on to the other one, he took a sip, and then to the third and he returned the glass back to me. I took another sip, as much as I was able. I passed it around again. The next man just took a little bit and said he didn't want any more, and so on. And I drank the whole of that glass full of this alcohol myself. And then the policeman took us off into another house which was empty. It didn't have a door. We were on the ground floor level of that house, and there were three rooms on the ground floor. They took me to the one furthest away, on the right-hand side, at the window to that room; that is to say, there was just a wooden frame round the window, and on the window there was just some plastic. In the room there were two mattresses, one on each side, and in another corner there was a small stove. The policeman whom I knew told us, "Don't anybody try to escape. You can't escape." And having drunk that alcohol, I began to regain consciousness. A boy was brought in after that, he was 14 or 15, he was barefoot, and the policeman asked him where he was from. He told him. He asked him his name. He asked him whether he knew a man, that is to say, a policeman who was that person's neighbour. He asked him whether he was hungry, the boy said yes. Then he said, "Take some tins and eat them." The young boy began to eat. He was frightened. Another policeman came in asking for that boy because allegedly the boy had wounded some policeman by the road. They began to beat him outside in the hallway. They took him off somewhere, they searched him for a rifle -- for a pistol, then they returned him, they brought him back. After a certain amount of time had passed, they brought in another man whom I knew as well. And later on they brought yet another man in whom I did not know, and the second policeman asked me whether I knew him and he asked me some other things from before the war. And later on they brought in another man; he was a Muslim whom I did know. We stayed there for some time. I talked to the policemen about the people -- to this one policeman about our common acquaintances. He would ask where they were, what they had been in the war, and he said, "See what your government has done to you. It's sold you out. Why didn't you stay with us?" I said that I didn't know. At one particular point I just said that I was just beginning to feel better and coming to, and he said, "Well, it's difficult." After some more time had gone by, another man came, I knew this man as well, and he said --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was this new man a Serb or a Muslim, this new arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was also a Serb and he came and said these four men should go downstairs, these other ones should stay where they are. So we left the house by the crossroads, we crossed over the road, and they took us to a warehouse of some kind which was situated on the banks of the River Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session briefly again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the witness could refer to Exhibit 178 again, which should be up there, and if we could put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, do you see on this photograph, 178, the area where the warehouse was that you were taken to that day? And could you point to it if you see it, just the general area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: You can't see the warehouse now. It was destroyed. There was never a petrol pump here before the war. He was here [indicates] -- it was here [indicates] in front of the petrol pump, this area here, the general area of the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That was built on part of the area where the warehouse stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, he's pointing to an area on the left-hand side of the photograph where you can just make out some big yellow bars which is a petrol station.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, you were taken to this very area by Mr. Ruez of the Office of the Prosecutor relatively recently, and you took him around to all these places, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What happened at this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When we went into the warehouse, before the war there was an agricultural chemist there, and the warehouse was 15 or 20 metres long, and you could buy medicines for agricultural purposes. When we entered, there were two rooms. One room actually was the entrance to the warehouse itself. So when I went into this smaller room, they started shouting at us, and (redacted) (redacted) And they started shouting, they said, "Take your clothes off." They began beating us. We took our clothes off and they lined us up along the wall. And while they were lining us up, I counted 12 people, Muslims, who were in their underpants. Their clothes had been taken off. I began to be afraid. I began to shake. He said, "Why are you shaking" and began to beat me. And I noticed a colleague of mine from the company I worked for, we worked together, amongst the Muslims, that is. And they beat us there, they inflicted blows on us, and we fell to the ground. And then a young man turned up. He was between 18 and 20 years old. I noticed him too. At the first point, he asked me where I was, what I had been doing, what I was (redacted) (redacted), "Why did you make these people take their clothes off? They are going to go for an exchange." He said, "They won't be exchanged, I'm going to kill them all," and a young man that I had buried some 40 days ago. And he said, "If anybody is going to kill them, I'll kill them. I did this 15 days ago." And then they hugged each other and went outside. Later on another man with a moustache came in, he was thin, and said, "Put your clothes on." The four of us dressed, began to dress. We took up our clothes. The other one said that they couldn't find their clothing, and he said he'd bring them some. And he went into some room and brought some clothing, as much as he was able to carry. The people then dressed themselves but they said, "This isn't my clothing," and he said, "Don't be choosey. Put anything you can find on because that's all there is." Then from that small room they transferred us into this larger room, which was where the shop was, and there were some bars there but no glass. They lined us up against the wall and beat us. I was beaten most and I was a little frightened. But after I had drunk the alcohol, I felt a bit better. Our hands had to be up against the wall and our stomachs had to be up against the wall. They hit me on my back, on my head, with their clubs or batons. Next to me throughout that time was my bag, and then he said, "Who does the bag belong to?" I said it belonged to me, that it was mine. He told me to turn around. I turned around, he said, "Open the bag and throw out the things you have in it." I did so. I threw them out onto the floor. There was a pair of trousers, a couple of T-shirts that I had taken with me, some bandages. I had some injections to stop bleeding, something like that, I got it from humanitarian aid, and I took this along with me just in case I happened to be wounded, so I could dress my wounds. Then he began to inflict wounds on me, he said, "What do you need that for?" I fell on the ground again, and they beat me again. And after some time a bus parked in front of the warehouse. There were no signs up on the bus. I wanted to try and remember, but there was nothing written up on the bus. It was driven by a blonde lady. I think she had a white shirt on and she had the sort of bicycle, short trousers on, she was wearing (redacted), come and board the bus. Put your hands behind your neck. Get into the bus, and don't you dare sit down. Don't any of you dare sit down." And as they were boarding the bus, and when I boarded the bus, my seat was at the back, and standing between the seats, I looked to the back of the bus and on the front door there were these two men, these uniformed people, and Deronjic was amongst them, two at the front and two at the back. And then I was wondering where this bus was going to go, and I thought, if it starts for Kravica, then that would be the end of it. But the bus moved towards Drinjaca. It wasn't a long ride. The bus stopped once again. And they put on the music in the bus louder, and when the bus stopped he told us to get out. We got out of the bus --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. Can you tell me -- I want to go back to the house where you were being beaten right before you got onto the bus. What were the people wearing that were beating you in that house? What kind of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They had camouflage military uniforms, trousers and the kinds of shirts they wear, and they had rifles with a folding butt, automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I think you mentioned, or it was at least translated as a baton. Do you remember being hit by anything that was like a baton, the kind that police carry, or was it just rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, they beat us with anything they could. He got hold of my hair and threw me down on the ground. My worst moment was when he stepped on my head in his army boots and pressed me down against the concrete. They beat us with all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you recall seeing any baton, a billy club, a stick, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The one with the moustache would come from time to time and I think he would go down there, underneath the warehouse, which is where there was a cellar of some kind, the cellar to this agricultural warehouse. He went down there. And I think that the people's clothes had been down there, people who had undressed. They asked for our valuables, for our money, asked who had taken our money. So this man with a moustache would come from time to time. He would go downstairs and then come up again.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I just want to identify, if I could, what kind of implements you were hit with. Did you see a stick or was it just rifles, or could you tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I saw the stick when he was carrying it. It was about 60 or 70 centimetres long. I think it was wooden. But they beat me most with rifle butts and the barrel, against my back, my head, and the spine.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you got on the bus, how many Serb soldiers were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The same soldiers who were beating us, they were the same ones. On the front door was the one I knew, and another one, and the other two, the one with the moustache and another one, were at the back door.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of those four soldiers were armed with weapons while they were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, they all had automatic rifles, with a folding or collapsible butt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could direct the witness to Exhibit 176, which may be up there already.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, if you could just take a look at that. Do you recall looking at this map last night and pointing out to a little area where the bus stopped, and do you see that area marked on this map that you pointed to last night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you point out the little area where the bus stopped now with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It is this yellow dot [indicates], on a large bend. To the right there's a river and to the left there's a parking area for one bus. But he stopped where there was a widening of the road. He crossed over to the other side of the road, and we got off then. And they lined us up next to the road and I was thinking of jumping over the fence of the road, but

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: the moustache said, "No, not there. Let them come down to the river." Then they told us to cross over --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Sorry, I just signalled for you to stop for a moment. Can you tell us how many Muslims got off that bus and were lined up there along the road, how many in number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were the 12 and us four, which makes it 16, and two of them stayed behind in the house and nothing is known about what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Including that person you described as a 15-year-old boy, he was with you outside the bus.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How many of the armed Serb soldiers were with you outside that bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In front of the bus or in the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Well, how many came to this spot with you? How many Serb soldiers came with you? I know four came with the bus. Any more than those four?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, no more. Just the four of them. And the bus just stopped, we got off, the bus moved forward, and I think that it later went back. It stopped just for a moment for us to get off.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then tell us what happened to you and the group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: As I said, they lined us up against this fence, but (redacted), the man with the moustache, said, "Not there. Let them come down." There was grass next to the road. We went downhill for some 15 or 20 metres, and then they lined us up alongside the river, and he told us that we should get to the river. I was somewhere in the middle of that line, so I was third in line towards the Jadar River. When we got there, we were lined up against the river bank. I was third from the left. To my left was the man I knew; behind me, I don't know how far, there was another one, two others at the other side. And we waited for our lives to end there, and we expected -- there was half a minute or a minute of silence, and just then the images of my children appeared in my mind and I thought I was done for. However, the man who was standing in front of me, he was hit here [indicates]. I saw the bullet pass through his shirt. I expected the shot to hit me. It hit me on the left hip and I threw myself into the river. I was wearing a leather jacket. My face was in the water, and I held my breath for as long as I could. I raised my head a little to catch some breath. He noticed me raising my head, and I felt the bullets whizzing around my head. I ducked under the water again. And then I got hold of a rock in the water with my hand, and unnoticed I turned my head to the left to catch some breath, and with my right hand I pulled myself to the centre of the river. I was wearing this leather jacket. It was blown up. And he perhaps didn't notice that I was turning around, though I did it as indiscernibly as I could. And then the current started carrying me down river, I let go and then I hit my head against a rock. Then I turned on my back and they saw that I had turned. They opened bursts of fire on me. I didn't believe I hadn't been hit. I just spread out my arms and let the current carry me. And they couldn't follow me any more because there was a small canyon, a hillside and a road and a concrete embankment. I thought I was dead. Again I raised my head and I saw them going back to the road. Later I got hold of a rock. I stood on it, I looked over my body to see whether there were any wounds in my stomach. I knew that I had been hit on the left side. I went out of the river, crossed the meadow, reached a water tank. I was terribly thirsty. On this tank there was a tap, and I went round this reservoir; there was no water. I had a big wound, so I tore up my shirt to be able to dress the wound but I couldn't. I dragged myself up higher, and there was a meadow there. And I saw a rather large building and I wondered what that could be. Before the war I knew there was a kind of TO barracks there of the former Yugoslavia, and looking through the woods I saw a monument. There used to be an old mosque there. And I spent two and a half hours there drying my clothes and thinking what I should do. I was bleeding heavily. I tried to move but it was difficult. And I was lucky that my bones were not fractured. So I broke off a wooden stick, put on my clothes, and continued uphill, partly through the meadows, partly through the woods --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness S. Let me interrupt you to go back and clarify a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 182.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness S, were you able to find the river bank with Mr. Ruez this summer and actually show him the spot where you believed this to have occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We found -- though at first we couldn't find it, and then they told me it was lower down. I told them, it can't be lower down because the tank is on the other side. We have to find it. And from that spot you can see the bend in the direction of Drinjaca. We went down to the river. They said, "It must be here." I said, "It can't be there." And then I recognised the path we took going down. But there is no widening of the road there. We saw a tree had fallen. Nobody could have cut it, just its branches had been cut. So when the water is high, it carries away whatever there is. So I think it must be here [indicates]. And from the other side of the road we saw that some water was coming through. There are two big rocks which I recognised very well because I hit my head against one of them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has pointed to the general rocky area by the bank of the river as the place he recalls this execution taking place. Could we also show the witness Exhibit 183, and I'm hoping we have a colour shot of that for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were wounded in the side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you bear the marks of those gunshots today, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You were shot in the back by the troops, were you not, the back and in the side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He hit me in my hip from behind, and the bullet passed right next to the bone and it cut through some tendons, so I couldn't walk properly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: We took a Polaroid photo of you today. I think that's upside down. Yes. Can you show us the entry wound, point that out for us? I know this isn't the best photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: This is the entry wound. It was much larger here [indicates], the exit wound. And when I was bandaging it, my whole fist could go inside. And my veins could be seen, the ligaments. And I thought to myself if the bone had been fractured, then I won't be able to get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, he pointed to a small area to the right side of the picture of a scar that he referred to as the entry wound, and then on the left side of the picture, a much larger scarred area that's been referred to as the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness S, in order to give you a chance so you can finish up today, I know that there's more to this story and that you survived a difficult hike through the woods and weren't able to get out to Nezuk until the 16th of July. But at this point I'm going to stop my questions so the Defence counsel can ask questions, and then of course the Judge will ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic, would you like to start and then we can see if you can finish, or you can continue tomorrow. You decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try, Mr. President, to finish today, bearing in mind what I have already notified you about, the medical treatment for General Krstic, but in any event to spare the witness coming into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: First of all, good afternoon, Witness S. Because of the protective measures, I can't address you by name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you had both professional and private contacts with Serbs before the outbreak of hostilities, or rather the conflict in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, very good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about those relationships, from your own personal experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I don't know which friends you're referring to, my friends or Serbs as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt. If you can let the witness know about being too particular about friends and things, because otherwise it will identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my learned friend. My question referred to very general relationships, no specific relations between the witness and his friends and acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I had very good relations with certain individuals and with my neighbours. We hear one another even today, with some of them. But there are others whom I knew very well as a child. I better not talk about any details, how we knew each other. If we go into closed session, I could tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness S, can it be said that those relations at the global level between Serbs and Muslims in the area, until the outbreak of hostilities, were correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, until up to a year before the actual beginning of the war, I did have good relations. But many friends surprised me who used to be on very good terms with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the cooling of relations on both sides occurred, as you say, about a year prior to the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: As I say, a year before the war. Though I still have friends that I communicate with, but after everything I've gone through, how can you trust them, and who can you trust? Just imagine a situation when you meet a man in the street every day, you say hello to him, and at the end he kills you just because you have a Muslim name. Is that the deign of a human being? I can understand some things, but some things I simply cannot. If I had been an important man, I might understand it. But for an ordinary citizen, with a secondary school education, I think there's absolutely no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, or rather the protected area of Srebrenica, was there any armed formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There was the Territorial Defence, and UNPROFOR -- there were people who had organised themselves in all the villages until UNPROFOR arrived. After UNPROFOR arrived, I don't know any more, I don't know that anything existed, but maybe -- there probably was but I'm not familiar. I was no longer in the Territorial Defence. I was in civilian. I engaged in various business activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the column that was formed in Susnjari? And who led that column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: What do you mean who led it? Let me tell you, it was a situation where people had no choice. You have death on one side and on the other. And there was no organisation, it was just an attempt to save one's life, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that a part of the column was armed with some kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They weren't really properly armed. They were just people who had weapons from before the war and those that found them during the war. You know very well that we had conflicts with the Serbs over Srebrenica before UNPROFOR arrived. We know very well what happened in Bratunac. And what should we have done? To wait for the same fate to befall us as in Bratunac, close the stadium and then call out people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. That part of the column, did it have a military leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Believe me, I am not aware of that. I was a civilian. I can't say what I don't know, but whatever I do know I will tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by these four officers, that conversation or interrogation, was it conducted in a correct manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On their part, yes. While we were there, nobody beat us or touched us. They gave us something to eat and to drink. I told you what happened at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I really don't want to remind you about that. Somebody mentioned that you should have been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. This young man of about 18 or 20, he was very young, he had short blue pants on, a belt, and a pistol in a leather holster, a blue T-shirt, a beret, and he said that to this man that I said I knew, and after all that they gave each other a hug and went out in front of the warehouse where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that somebody prevented him from carrying out this idea of an exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: You mean somebody who would not allow us to be exchanged? I really don't think that he had the power to do anything, in view of the other people I saw. He was a young man of 18 or 20. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. Witness S, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell us what time the execution occurred by the banks of the Jadar River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was in the morning, between 9.00 and 11.00 or 12.00. I don't know exactly because when this was happening to me, when I got out near the reservoir, my watch had stopped. Maybe it had stopped while I was being beaten. But anyway, it all happened before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On July 13th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for one last question, for the same reason we've been going into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness S, I would like to ask you one question which you passed quickly. You said when you were interrogated by these four men in uniform, the policemen, you saw 12 buses coming with the women and children. What happened to these 12 buses? Do you have an idea of where they took them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: At that time those policemen who were wearing blue camouflage uniforms were not questioning us. But the four men who I assume were officers, military officers, they gave us to eat and then they told us, "Turn around to face the road." We did and we saw these buses. They were not overcrowded, there were as many people as there were seats, and they told us, as I have already said, "You see how we treat your people properly." And those buses went off towards Milici, Vlasenica, and on from there. We just saw them for a moment because we had to turn back to face them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you don't know what happened to the buses, or to the people inside the buses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about these military people who were questioning you? Did you notice any insignia on their clothes, what division they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They didn't have any insignia. There was something in me, there was hope in me that I would survive all that, I had some strength of some sorts. But I didn't notice any insignia because their sleeves were rolled up, and one had even buttoned his sleeve up there. So there were no ranks or anything on their chests, around the pockets or on the sleeves, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, apart from the questions that were asked of you, would you like to add anything? Is there something you would like to say independently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding everything, or regarding just my statement and my own experiences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Regarding everything, and your experience. It has to be relevant to what's happening in your part of the world.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think after all this, the most important thing is that I have survived, though my health is poor. I have come here to tell the truth, and I thank the attorneys of the accused who treated me correctly, and everyone else. I would like to appeal to this Tribunal, if it can, to bring the people who did this to me so that I can look them in the face and we can clear everything up, and for Attorney Petrusic to be there too so I can tell him how this could have happened. When you meet somebody in the street every day and say hello and then he turns around and kills you, it's something I find incomprehensible. And I think friendship with those people who did this to me is over forever. That's as much as I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And now you can be taken out. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do have some exhibits, Your Honour. We want to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You want to tender some exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to tender some exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you know that the accused has to leave. Shall we allow him to leave and we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the Defence has no objection, yes. This shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. So we'll ask for the accused to be taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you want a closed session or an open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, an open session. No problem. They are Exhibits 176, 177, 178, 182, and 183. I can describe them if counsel wishes but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection to the documents tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So please tender them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would tender those, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, do you have any exhibits to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in relation to this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to thank both the Prosecutor and the Defence counsel for this prompt day, trial day. We will resume tomorrow at 9.30.
